text: Now, a mistake: leaving out the checking look. Listing the looks on paper sounds slow. Many developers skip it and start with the looks they can think of. An empty box, a typed box, and a done message. Here is the mock they write. Compare this with our form a moment ago. Line eight is a plain input. Nothing turns it off. And on line nine, the button is disabled only when status is empty. The note on that line is marked wrong. There's no checking look, so Apply stays on while the server checks. Later, when the handler is connected, this page works fine for a calm shopper. But here's what happens to an impatient one. The shopper types welcome and clicks Apply. There's no checking look, so nothing turns the box or Apply off. The server needs one and a half seconds. The shopper sees no change and clicks Apply again. So the form is sent a second time, and the code goes to the server twice. Ugh. Writing the list of looks first shows the gap. Between typing and success, the shopper waits. The React docs list this waiting look on its own. Submitting. Form is completely disabled, spinner is shown. Their page on batching also notes that if the first button click disables a form, the second click would not submit it again. Once the checking look is on the list, the mock has to say what it looks like. That's why our mock turns off the box and Apply when status is checking. Which looks did the developer list? That's the question figure fifteen asks with two sides. On one side, three looks: empty, typing, success. There's no look for the wait, so Apply stays on while the server checks, and a second click sends the code twice. On the other side, five looks: empty, typing, checking, error, success. The wait is its own look. The box and Apply are off while checking, and a second click does nothing. Computer science has a name for something that is always in exactly one of a few states, like our box with its five looks. It's called a state machine. You'll hear the name in interviews. The React docs say React stands at the intersection of design and computer science, and this method takes one idea from each side, the designer's list of looks and the state machine. So that's principle two, visual states. List every look before any logic. Write down every look the user can see, then draw each one from a single status prop before adding state or handlers. It's so tempting to jump straight into handlers, but the look you forget to list is exactly the look you forget to build, and the waiting look is the one everybody forgets. Then the button stays on while the server thinks, and the impatient user clicks twice. With a status prop and a default value, you can switch the whole component between its looks by changing one word. And with Map, you can see every look on one page. The good version takes status with a default of empty, because one prop picks the look. If status is success, it returns the free delivery line. Otherwise, it returns Apply, turned off when status is empty or checking. The version to avoid turns Apply off only when status is empty. There's no checking look, so Apply stays on while the server checks. Section three. Principle three, find every trigger. A button that changes back on its own. So far, our looks change only when we edit the code. But on a real page, something has to move the component from one look to the next. Here is a small example with two kinds of movement. A copy link button shows copied for a moment after a click, then it goes back to copy link. We leave out the copying itself here because only the label matters. A brand-new component now, CopyButton.jsx, and the whole thing fits in twelve lines. Line one imports useState from React. On line four, we keep one piece of state called status with its setter, setStatus. It starts as ready. Then comes the click handler, handleClick. Line seven calls setStatus with copied, and the note on that line says it's moved by the user's click. Line eight is the interesting one. It calls setTimeout with a small function that sets status back to ready after fifteen hundred milliseconds. The note says, "Moved by a timer one and a half seconds later." And line eleven returns the button. Its onClick is handleClick, and its label checks status. If status is copied, it shows copied. Otherwise, copy link. When the page opens, status is ready, so the button says copy link. Over in the browser, figure sixteen. A browser window at localhost five one seven three, and one button in it reading copy link. This is the page right when it opens. Now the user clicks it once. Same window, same button, right after the click. The label now says, "Copied." That's figure seventeen. Then the user does nothing at all, and one and a half seconds later, the button changes back. Wait a moment, and the button reads, "Copy link" again. That's figure eighteen. Nobody clicked a second time. One and a half seconds just passed, and it went back by itself. So here is what happened in order. Everything begins with the user's click, and React calls handleClick. Calling setStatus with copied asks for the copied look. Then setTimeout, from lesson fifteen, asks the browser to run a small function after fifteen hundred milliseconds. The handler finishes, and React draws the button with the label copied. One and a half seconds later, the timer ends, and the browser runs that small function. It calls setStatus with ready, and React draws the button again with the label Copy Link. So two different things moved this button. The first was the user's click. The second was a timer, and nobody touched anything for it. The React docs give these two kinds of trigger names. So there are two kinds. A human input is something the user does: clicking a button, typing in a box, following a link. The docs note that human inputs often require event handlers. And a computer input is something that happens without the user: a network answer arriving, a timer ending, an image finishing loading. The docs draw a finger for human inputs and a row of ones and zeros for computer inputs. Then they add the rule that matters most. In both cases, you must set state variables to update the UI.
